title: Stoic Oikeiōsis — how concern can grow beyond the self
when: Developed in early Stoicism, founded by Zeno of Citium around 300 BCE; its surviving accounts are later reports and Roman-era adaptations, so the doctrine’s precise early formulation remains uncertain.
people: Zeno of Citium, Chrysippus, Hierocles, Cicero, Seneca
origin: Hellenistic Greek philosophy, especially the Athenian Stoic school; later discussed and adapted in Roman philosophy.
idea: Oikeiōsis (often translated “appropriation,” “affiliation,” or “familiarization”) describes how a creature first recognizes its own constitution as belonging to it and is naturally moved to preserve it. Stoic accounts extend the idea through human development: reason reshapes our impulses, while our natural sociability widens concern from ourselves to family and community, potentially to all humanity. This does not mean that every person is automatically virtuous, nor that the early Stoics left us an uncontested argument. Their works largely survive through fragments and later authors, and scholars debate how exactly self-concern grounds justice. Still, the concept gives Stoicism a distinctive picture of ethical growth: moral life is not simply self-denial, but a widening and rational education of what we count as “our own.”
relevance: In an age of polarized identities and global interdependence, oikeiōsis asks how attention and responsibility might expand without pretending that care for close relationships must disappear. It also invites scrutiny: does natural human sociability genuinely support universal obligations, and how far should our circle of concern extend beyond our species?
